YouTube doesn't act arbitrarily as you're implying. They have an established process that allows users to dispute unlawful takedown requests such as, for instance, false copyright claims - that culminates in legal action if Rockstar persists. Here is an overview of the process and usage rights, from the EFF. Victims of the potentially questionable claims could file counter-claims and Rockstar would be left to deal with it in the courts or the video would go back up.

Correct, they do have a process for dealing with copyright. wherein the final word as to weather a work is infringing is given to the company claiming infringements. The "Counter Claims" are reviewed by the company making the claim itself, at least in the case of contentID, which is the only system that uses the terminology. As a contentID flag is not a legal proceeding, but instead an internal process, google and rockstar may, from a legal perspective, do what they wish in regards to it. Things don't get official until a DMCA takedown request enters the process. At that point, in order to maintain its safe harbor status, youtube will take the video down immediately, waiting for the uploader to make a counter claim. That is the first point a human other than the uploader will EVER look at a video for any reason. Now, if the content holder (for lack of a better term) wants to file suit to keep it down, they are free to do so, but you still can't sue for a false claim. Youtube can also, seeing as its their service, simply take down a video that they consider borderline, without it becoming litigious, which is far from unheard of. Issues involving youtube videos will never see the courtroom.

Once again there is a very well established order of operations. YouTube does not act arbitrarily as a rule. The EFF page I referenced lays it out clearly and visually. In the case of contentID it is:

  • 1. Content ID match. The video is removed.
  • 2. The user can dispute this claim or accept it and move on.
  • 3. If disputed the rightsholder must determine if the claim is genuine. This is sometimes the first step where an actual human looks at what's supposedly infringing. The rightsholder can release the claim or uphold it.
  • 4. The user can dispute the claim if the rightsholder upholds it.
  • 5. Now at this point the rightsholder must either release the claim or file a DMCA takedown.

At that point it does become a legal issue. And yes, cases have made it to court. In particular the dancy baby case: Lenz vs Universal Music Corp. A user got the EFF involved after Universal Music started filing copyright claims on all videos using Prince's music without consideration of fair use. Universal Music lost. All in all it's a reasonable and fair system. The user is guilty until proven innocent, but given there may be thousands of infringers to one rightsholder that's probably fair as the reverse would arguably impose an unreasonable burden on the rightsholder.

If you're going to a college that isn't too far away, it would be helpful to spend some time in the city and around campus. Get to know the lay of the land, learn where the nearest grocery and convenience stores are to campus, figure out which local bars are 18+ rather than 21+, learn which restaurants are open all night, and maybe even memorize some of the university campus. That becomes very helpful when you get to school, because you'll be so busy signing up for and finding your classes and figuring the basic things out that you won't have time to look for these places. If you know it already, you can help other people and become friends with them on the way.

Otherwise, if you have a shot at any summer job, go for it. Don't spend the money on restaurants (EXCEPT for dates, you can spend however much you want on those); go for the grocery store or whatever cheap meal plan you are stuck with. Use that as "get around town" money to help build a social life and stuff.
